cards.q: Which of these contactor auxiliary contacts is normally closed?
cards.why: The second digits give the function: 1–2 normally closed, 3–4 normally open. The first digit only numbers the contact.

cards.q: Under a coil, the contact table shows `13–14 /7.5`. What does that mean?
options: That coil's NO contact is used on page 7, column 5
The coil itself is drawn on page 7, column 5
It is terminal 5 on terminal strip X7
Contact 7.5 of the coil is normally closed
cards.why: The table under a coil points to where each of its contacts is used: page 7, column 5. The contact there points back to the coil.

cards.q: A pressure switch is drawn with a normally closed contact. In service the pressure is high enough to operate it. What is the contact doing?
options: Closed, as drawn
Closed: NC means always closed
It depends on the wire colour
Open
cards.why: Drawings show devices at rest: no pressure. Operated by the pressure, the NC contact opens.

cards.q: A machine started faulting this morning. What do you do first?
options: Replace the part that is most likely to have failed
Reload the PLC program from the last backup
Ask the operator, and read the alarm history
Strip down the area where the machine stops
cards.why: Evidence is free and narrows the search: what happened, when, and what changed.

cards.q: {n} contacts are in series and one is open. With half-splitting, how many tests at most will find it?
cards.why: Each test in the middle halves the suspects: $\log_2 n$, rounded up. 8: 3; 16: 4; 20: 5; 50: 6; 100: 7.

cards.q: An overload keeps tripping on a conveyor. Someone turned the setting up and the trips stopped. What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing: the trips have stopped
The cause is still there, unfixed
Only the maker may set an overload
The overload now trips too quickly
cards.why: The overload was warning that the motor works too hard. Turning it up hides the cause and removes the motor's protection.

cards.q: What is the difference between a FAT and a SAT?
options: FAT at the builder's works; SAT on site
FAT tests the electrics; SAT tests the software
FAT is done by the customer; SAT by the builder
They are two names for exactly the same test
cards.why: Factory acceptance test: prove as much as possible before shipping, when changes are cheap. Site acceptance test: prove it works installed, with real services and product.

cards.q: A loop check: a transmitter is ranged 0 to {span} bar. You inject {ma} mA. What should SCADA show, in bar?
cards.why: 4–20 mA spans 16 mA: the reading is $\frac{mA - 4}{16}$ of the span. 12 mA is half way.

cards.q: An I/O check proves each field device reaches the right PLC tag. What does it not prove?
options: That the wiring is right
That the tags are named as on the I/O list
That the device works at all
That the control logic does the right thing
cards.why: I/O checks prove the connections, point by point. The sequences, interlocks and alarms are proved by functional tests afterwards.

cards.q: What is a functional design specification (FDS)?
options: The list of every signal and its address
The price and delivery terms of the job
How the system will work, agreed before coding
The operators' daily start-up checklist
cards.why: The FDS says how the system will meet the customer's needs, agreed before programming, so everyone builds and tests against the same thing.

cards.q: Which of these does an I/O list hold for each signal?
options: Its price and its supplier
Its tag, type, range and address
The operator's name and shift
Its fault and repair history
cards.why: One row per signal: tag, description, type (DI, DO, AI, AO), range and units, PLC address, and the device it comes from.

cards.q: Match each document with its job.
pairs: How the system will meet it
How to operate and maintain it
cards.why: Needs, then design, then the detail, then the handover.

cards.q: What goes in a technical report's summary?
options: The problem, the findings, the recommendation
The detailed method and the equipment list
The background to the job and who asked for it
The appendices and the page numbers of each section
cards.why: A few lines for the reader who reads nothing else. The detail goes in the body and appendices.

cards.q: Put the parts of a technical report in order.
cards.why: Summary first for the busy reader; then what and why, how, what you found, what it means, what to do; raw data at the back.

cards.q: How do a report's results differ from its discussion?
options: Results always come after the discussion in a report
They are one section under two names
The discussion holds the raw data tables
Results give the facts; discussion what they mean
cards.why: Keep them apart: results are the facts, the discussion the interpretation, so a reader can check one against the other.

cards.q: Mid-project, a customer adds work but keeps the same deadline and price. What should happen?
options: Do the extra work quietly to keep them happy
Refuse all changes once the project has started
Raise a change and agree time or cost first
Cut the testing time to make room for it
cards.why: Scope, time and cost are tied. A change request agrees what shifts before the work is done.

cards.q: Task A takes {a} days. Then tasks B ({b} days) and C ({c} days) run at the same time. Then task D takes {d} days. What is the shortest time for the project, in days?
cards.why: D waits for the longer of B and C: that chain is the critical path. The shorter one has slack.

cards.q: A task has three days of slack (float). What does that mean?
options: It must finish three days before its deadline
It can slip three days without moving the finish
It needs three more people to finish on time
It is on the critical path of the project
cards.why: Tasks on the critical path have no slack: any delay there moves the finish date.

cards.q: Two engineers work a job for {h} hours each at £{r} an hour each. A {p}% overhead is added to labour. What is the labour cost, in £?
cards.why: Two people × hours × rate = 2 × {h} × £{r}, then add the overhead: × (1 + {p}/100).

cards.q: Materials cost £{m}. You add a {p}% markup. What do you charge for them, in £?
cards.why: Markup is a percentage added to the cost: cost × (1 + p/100).

cards.q: A job costs £{c} to do. What price gives a {g}% margin (profit as a percentage of the price), in £?
cards.why: Margin is profit ÷ price, so cost = price × (1 − margin): price = $\frac{cost}{1 - margin}$. A 25% margin is a 33% markup, not 25%.

cards.q: What is a good way to teach an apprentice a new task?
options: Explain, show, watch them do it, then practise
Hand over the manual and leave them to read it
Always do it yourself so it is done right
Let them try first without saying anything
cards.why: Explain, demonstrate, then let them do it with you there, and give feedback while they practise.

cards.q: Which is the most useful feedback?
options: "Great work, the whole panel looks spot on"
"Neater next time, it could be tidier overall"
"Good effort overall, keep it going like that"
"Terminations tight; sleeve the next ones too"
cards.why: Useful feedback is specific, about the work not the person, and says what to do next.

cards.q: Why ask an apprentice "what would you check next?" rather than tell them?
options: It saves you having to know the answer
It is quicker than telling them outright
It makes them think, and shows what they know
It avoids you taking any responsibility
cards.why: Open questions build their reasoning, and their answers tell you where to help.

cards.q: How should a presentation to a customer start?
options: With the full history of the project
With the point, and why it matters to them
With a long list of the technical terms
With who is on the team and an agenda slide
cards.why: Busy people decide in the first minute whether to listen. Lead with the conclusion, then support it.

cards.q: What makes good slides for a customer meeting?
options: One idea each, few words, and pictures
Every word you plan to say, in full
As many slides as possible, to show effort
Small text, so that everything fits
cards.why: Slides support what you say; if they hold the whole script, people read instead of listening.

cards.q: A customer asks a question you cannot answer. What do you do?
options: Give a confident guess to keep their trust
Change the subject to something you know
Say it is covered in the manual and move on
Say so, and promise an answer by a set time
cards.why: A wrong answer costs more trust than an honest "I'll find out", provided you do.
